claim: Anthropogenic pressures are shifting the composition of reef primary producer communities from calcifying to non-calcifying organisms globally.
source: Anthropogenic pressures are shifting the composition of reef primary producer communities from calcifying to non-calcifying organisms globally (Cinner et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cinner et al., 2016 and Smith et al., 2016

claim: Fleshy algae gain competitive advantage over corals through their interaction with heterotrophic microbes.
source: These changes occur as fleshy algae gain competitive advantage over corals through their interaction with heterotrophic microbes (Barott and Rohwer, 2012; Jorissen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barott and Rohwer, 2012 and Jorissen et al., 2016

claim: High Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC) release rates by fleshy algae stimulate overgrowth of heterotrophic bacteria.
source: High Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC) release rates by fleshy algae stimulate overgrowth of heterotrophic bacteria (Haas et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2013

claim: Exacerbated heterotrophic growth creates hypoxic zones at the coral-algae interface that kill corals.
source: The exacerbated heterotrophic growth creates hypoxic zones at the coral-algae interface that kill corals (Haas et al., 2013a; Haas et al., 2014b; Roach et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2013a; Haas et al., 2014b; Roach et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2006

claim: Algae dominance stimulates heterotrophic bacteria in the water above the reef and leads to an increase in microbial biomass and energetic demands.
source: At the reef-scale, algae dominance stimulates heterotrophic bacteria in the water above the reef and leads to an increase in microbial biomass and energetic demands, described as reef microbialization (Haas et al., 2016; McDole et al., 2012; Silveira et al., 2015; Silveira et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2016; McDole et al., 2012; Silveira et al., 2015; Silveira et al., 2017

claim: Overgrowth of heterotrophic bacteria creates a feedback loop of coral death, opening space for more algae overgrowth and microbial biomass accumulation.
source: Overgrowth of heterotrophic bacteria creates a feedback loop of coral death, opening space for more algae overgrowth and microbial biomass accumulation (Dinsdale and Rohwer, 2011; Rohwer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dinsdale and Rohwer, 2011; Rohwer et al., 2002

claim: Calcifying organisms invest 50% to 80% of their daily fixed carbon in respiration to sustain the energetic costs of calcification.
source: Calcifying organisms, including scleractinian corals and crustose coralline algae (CCA), invest 50% to 80% of their daily fixed carbon in respiration to sustain the energetic costs of calcification (Hatcher, 1988; Houlbrèque and Ferrier-Pagès, 2009; Tremblay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hatcher, 1988; Houlbrèque and Ferrier-Pagès, 2009; Tremblay et al., 2012

claim: Fleshy macroalgae allocate 10% to 30% to respiration, and release up to 60% of their primary production as dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the water.
source: Fleshy macroalgae allocate 10% to 30% to respiration, and release up to 60% of their primary production as dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the water (Cheshire et al., 1996; Crossland, 1987; Jokiel and Morrissey, 1986; Peninsula et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheshire et al., 1996; Crossland, 1987; Jokiel and Morrissey, 1986; Peninsula et al., 2007

claim: Fleshy algae allocate a higher proportion of their daily synthesized carbon to biomass compared to corals.
source: Fleshy algae also allocate a higher proportion of their daily synthesized carbon to biomass compared to corals, sustaining high herbivory pressure (Duarte and Cebrián, 1996; Falkowski et al., 1984; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duarte and Cebrián, 1996; Falkowski et al., 1984; Tremblay et al., 2016

claim: The ratio between DOC and O2 released by fleshy algae in bottle incubations is higher compared to corals.
source: Together, these processes are predicted to increase DOC-to-O2 ratios in coral exudates compared to algae, but experimental data have shown the opposite to be true: the ratio between DOC and O2 released by fleshy algae in bottle incubations is higher compared to corals (Haas et al., 2013b; Haas et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2013b; Haas et al., 2011

claim: Heterotrophic microbes growing on algal exudates produce fewer cells per unit of carbon consumed compared to growth on coral exudates.
source: Heterotrophic microbes growing on algal exudates produce fewer cells per unit of carbon consumed compared to growth on coral exudates (Haas et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2013; Silveira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2013; Silveira et al., 2015

claim: Microbes growing on algae-dominated reefs shift their metabolism from classic glycolysis (Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway, EMP) towards Pentose Phosphate (PP) and Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathways.
source: Microbes growing on algae-dominated reefs shift their metabolism from classic glycolysis (Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway, EMP) towards Pentose Phosphate (PP) and Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathways (Haas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haas et al., 2016

claim: The classic glycolic pathway generates more ATP and consumes more oxygen, while ED and PP leave a higher fraction of electrons accumulated as biomass.
source: These reduced coenzymes have different fates in the cell, and as a result, the classic glycolic pathway generates more ATP and consumes more oxygen, while ED and PP leave a higher fraction of electrons accumulated as biomass (Fuhrer and Sauer, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuhrer and Sauer, 2009

claim: Microbes found in microbialized reefs have different oxygen consumption rates when compared to healthy reefs.
source: These differences predict that microbes found in microbialized reefs have different oxygen consumption rates when compared to healthy reefs (Flamholz et al., 2013; Stettner and Segrè, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Flamholz et al., 2013; Stettner and Segrè, 2013

claim: Fleshy turf and macroalgae release up to three times more O2 in the surrounding seawater than calcifying organisms.
source: Fleshy turf and macroalgae release up to three times more O2 in the surrounding seawater than calcifying organisms (Haas et al., 2011; Naumann et al., 2010; Nelson et al., 2013; Silveira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2011; Naumann et al., 2010; Nelson et al., 2013; Silveira et al., 2015

claim: Algae-dominated systems have consistently lower O2 standing stocks.
source: Yet, algae-dominated systems have consistently lower O2 standing stocks (Calhoun et al., 2017; Haas et al., 2013b; Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calhoun et al., 2017; Haas et al., 2013b; Martinez et al., 2012

claim: Fleshy algae can produce O2 bubbles through heterogeneous nucleation resulting from O2 super-saturation at the algae's surface.
source: Fleshy algae can produce O2 bubbles through heterogeneous nucleation resulting from O2 super-saturation at the algae's surface (Kraines et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kraines et al., 1996

claim: The gaseous O2 in bubbles is not detected by dissolved O2 instruments, and may cause underestimation of autotrophy in oxygen-based primary productivity methods.
source: The gaseous O2 in bubbles is not detected by dissolved O2 instruments, and may cause underestimation of autotrophy in oxygen-based primary productivity methods (Atkinson and Grigg, 1984; Kraines et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atkinson and Grigg, 1984; Kraines et al., 1996

claim: Several studies recognize bubble formation on algal surfaces in benthic ecosystems.
source: While several studies recognize bubble formation on algal surfaces in benthic ecosystems, the fraction of photosynthetic oxygen lost as bubbles from coral reef primary producers has never been quantified (Freeman et al., 2018; Odum and Odum, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2018; Odum and Odum, 1955

claim: The fraction of photosynthetic oxygen lost as bubbles from coral reef primary producers has never been quantified.
source: While several studies recognize bubble formation on algal surfaces in benthic ecosystems, the fraction of photosynthetic oxygen lost as bubbles from coral reef primary producers has never been quantified (Freeman et al., 2018; Odum and Odum, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2018; Odum and Odum, 1955

claim: Fleshy macroalgae and microbes remove larger amounts of photosynthetic O2 by ebullition and respiration compared to corals.
source: The analysis of organic carbon consumption pathways encoded in bacterial metagenomes from 87 reefs in the Atlantic and Pacific combined with experimental quantification of cell-specific DOC and oxygen consumption showed that fleshy macroalgae and microbes remove larger amounts of photosynthetic O2 by ebullition and respiration compared to corals.
evidence: Supported by metagenomic data and experimental measurements described in the manuscript

claim: Microbial biomass in the reef boundary layer increased with fleshy algae cover.
source: In our dataset, microbial biomass in the reef boundary layer increased with fleshy algae cover (linear regression, p=6.25 x 10-8, R2 = 0.29).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the dataset (linear regression with p-value and R-squared)

claim: The relative abundance of genes encoding rate-limiting enzymes of central carbon metabolism could explain 14.3% of the variance in fleshy algae cover.
source: The relative abundance of these genes could explain 14.3% of the variance in fleshy algae cover.
evidence: Supported by random forest regression analysis results

claim: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, aspartate aminotransferase, oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase and KDPG aldolase genes had highest and significant explanatory power in predicting fleshy algae cover.
source: The genes with highest and significant explanatory power in the permutation test were phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, aspartate aminotransferase, oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase and KDPG aldolase (Figure 1 displays the enzyme genes with highest explanatory power according to their increasing mean squared error: 53.54%, 22.03%, 23.99%, 26.08% and 17.89%, and permutation test p-values = 0.009, 0.01, 0.03, 0.01 and 0.03, respectively; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis with permutation test p-values

claim: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase and aspartate aminotransferase are involved in anaplerotic routes, reactions that replenish the Krebs cycle when its intermediaries are diverted for biosynthesis.
source: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase and aspartate aminotransferase are involved in anaplerotic routes, reactions that replenish the Krebs cycle when its intermediaries are diverted for biosynthesis.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge of enzyme functions

claim: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase shunts glucose to both Entner-Doudoroff and Pentose Phosphate pathways.
source: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase shunts glucose to both Entner-Doudoroff and Pentose Phosphate pathways, and KDPG aldolase is unique to the Entner-Doudoroff pathway.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge of enzyme functions

claim: KDPG aldolase is unique to the Entner-Doudoroff pathway.
source: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase shunts glucose to both Entner-Doudoroff and Pentose Phosphate pathways, and KDPG aldolase is unique to the Entner-Doudoroff pathway.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge of enzyme functions

claim: Four enzyme genes (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, aspartate aminotransferase, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase, and KDPG aldolase) had a positive relationship with fleshy algae cover and participate in pathways of incomplete carbon oxidation.
source: These four enzyme genes had a positive relationship with fleshy algae cover (identified by random forest by their increasing mean squared error, followed by permutation test with p-values p=0.009, 0.01, 0.01 and 0.03, respectively), and participate in pathways of incomplete carbon oxidation, that is, lower oxygen consumption.
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis with permutation test p-values and biochemical knowledge

claim: Oxoglutarate dehydrogenase relative abundance had an inverse relationship with fleshy algae cover.
source: Oxoglutarate dehydrogenase relative abundance had an inverse relationship with fleshy algae cover (random forest increasing mean squared error, p=0.03).
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis with permutation test p-value

claim: Oxoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyzes an oxidative decarboxylation step in the Krebs cycle.
source: This enzyme catalyzes an oxidative decarboxylation step in the Krebs cycle, a pathway that produces most of the NADH that fuels oxygen consumption by oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge of enzyme function

claim: The bacterial community is being increasingly selected for pathways related to overflow metabolism and incomplete carbon oxidation at high algal cover.
source: These results suggest that the bacterial community is being increasingly selected for pathways related to overflow metabolism and incomplete carbon oxidation at high algal cover, which would predict a decoupling between organic carbon and oxygen consumption rates by microbes.
evidence: Inferred from the metagenomic data showing changes in enzyme gene abundances

claim: The gene rpoB (RNA polymerase) did not vary in relative abundance across the algal cover gradient.
source: The gene rpoB (RNA polymerase) was used as a control and did not vary in relative abundance across the algal cover gradient (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: Genes involved in oxidative stress did not show significant relationships with algal cover.
source: Genes involved in oxidative stress did not show significant relationships either.
evidence: Supported by analysis of metagenomic data

claim: Seven bacterial species significantly changed in abundance across the algae cover gradient.
source: Seven species significantly changed in abundance across the algae cover gradient (Figure 1—source data 1, Prochlorococcus marinus, Fibrisoma limi, Prolixibacter bellariivorans, Pelagibacter ubique, Ruegeria mobilis, Phaeobacter italicus, and Psychrobacter pacificensis).
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis of taxonomic data

claim: Five bacterial genera (Prochlorococcus, Thermotoga, Methanobacterium, Leuconostoc, and Rhodopirellula) changed their abundance with increasing fleshy algae cover.
source: At the genus level, five taxa (Prochlorococcus, Thermotoga, Methanobacterium, Leuconostoc, and Rhodopirellula) changed their abundance with increasing fleshy algae cover.
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis of taxonomic data

claim: There was no significant relationship between the abundances of Prochlorococcus and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase.
source: However, there was no significant relationship between the abundances of Prochlorococcus and oxogluratae dehydrogenase (p=0.26 in the linear regression of oxoglutarate dehydrogenase and log10-transformed Prochlorococcus abundance).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis with p-value

claim: The amount of DOC consumed per cell was higher in fleshy macroalgae treatments compared to coral and control treatments.
source: The amount of DOC consumed per cell was higher, that is, low cell yields per carbon consumed, in fleshy macroalgae treatments compared to coral and control treatments (Figure 2A, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(2)=13.7, p=0.001; Wilcoxon, p=0.005 and 0.008 for pairwise comparisons of algae vs controls and corals, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with statistical tests

claim: The amount of O2 consumed per cell was not different between coral, algae, and control treatments.
source: However, the amount of O2 consumed per cell was not different between treatments (Figure 2B, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(2)=0.5, p=0.77).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical tests

claim: The change in bacterial abundance in all primary producer bottles was higher compared to controls.
source: The change in bacterial abundance in all primary producer bottles was higher compared to controls (Figure 3A, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(4)=20.6, p=0.0003, Wilcoxon p=0.04, 0.02. 0.02. and 0.02 for pairwise comparisons of coral, CCA, turf and macroalgae against control, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical tests

claim: The change in bacterial abundance was higher in fleshy algae treatments compared to calcifying treatments.
source: The change in abundance was higher in fleshy algae treatments compared to calcifying treatments (Kruskal-Wallis χ2(2)=19.1, p=6.9×10−5, Wilcoxon p=0.001 for pairwise comparison of fleshy vs calcifying).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: Microbial cell volume changed differently in treatments during incubations.
source: Microbial cell volume changed differently in treatments during incubations (Figure 3B, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(5)=1235.2, p<2×10−16, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical tests

claim: Bacteria growing in control bottles showed no change in volume.
source: Bacteria growing in control bottles showed no change in volume (Wilcoxon, p=0.56 for pairwise comparison of control vs T0h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical test

claim: Cell volume decreased when bacteria grew on coral and CCA exudates, but increased when growing on turf and macroalgae exudates.
source: Cell volume decreased when bacteria grew on coral and CCA exudates, but increased when growing on turf and macroalgae exudates, and showed no change in controls (Wilcoxon p<2×10−16 for all pairwise comparisons vs T0h and vs control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: The change in total bacterial biomass was significantly different among treatments.
source: When taking abundance and cell volume into account, the change in total bacterial biomass was significantly different among treatments (Figure 3C, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(4)=21.6, p=0.0002, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical tests

claim: Coral exudates decreased total bacterial biomass, while turf and macroalgae increased total bacterial biomass, and CCA lead to no change.
source: Coral exudates decreased total bacterial biomass, while turf and macroalgae increased total bacterial biomass, and CCA lead to no change (Wilcoxon, p<0.05 for pairwise comparisons of coral, turf and macroalgae vs control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: The change in biomass in the two fleshy algae together was greater than in the calcifying organisms together.
source: The change in biomass in the two fleshy algae together was greater than in the calcifying organisms together (Kruskal-Wallis χ2(2)=19.1, p=7.1×10−5; Wilcoxon, p=0.0005 for pairwise comparison of fleshy vs calcifying).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: The pattern of higher biomass change in fleshy algae was observed in two independent experiments performed in different locations with distinct sets of primary producers.
source: This same pattern was observed in two independent experiments, one performed in the island of Curaçao, in the Caribbean (Figure 3) and one performed at the Hawaiian Institute of Marine Biology (HIMB, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), with distinct sets of primary producers, suggesting that this result may be broadly applicable to other reefs (Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two independent experiments shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Net dissolved O2 production was significantly different among primary producer treatments.
source: Net dissolved O2 production was significantly different among primary producer treatments (Figure 4A, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(4)=19.5, p=0.0006, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A with statistical tests

claim: Primary producers showed higher net dissolved O2 production compared to controls.
source: Primary producers showed higher net dissolved O2 production compared to controls (Wilcoxon with FDR-corrected pairwise comparisons p=0.004, 0.01, 0.01, 0.004 for comparisons between controls vs coral, CCA, turf and macroalgae, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: Net dissolved O2 production was not significantly different between fleshy and calcifying organisms.
source: Net dissolved O2 production was lower in macroalgae incubations, but not significantly different between fleshy and calcifying organisms (5.99 ± 2.29 and 6.33 ± 2.20 μmol cm−2 day−1 for fleshy and calcifying organisms, respectively, mean ± SE; Wilcoxon p=0.68).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical test

claim: There was a significant difference between gaseous O2 production observed in most primary producer bottles, while no gas was observed in control bottles.
source: There was a significant difference between gaseous O2 production observed in most primary producer bottles, while no gas was observed in control bottles (Figure 4B, Kruskal-Wallis χ2(4)=30.2, p=4.361e-06, Wilcoxon p=0.03, 0.002, 0.002, and 0.002 for pairwise comparisons between controls vs corals, CCA, turf and macroalgae, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with statistical tests

claim: Fleshy organisms produced significantly more gaseous O2 than calcifying organisms.
source: Fleshy organisms produced significantly more gaseous O2 than calcifying organisms (0.42 ± 0.35 and 2.33 ± 1.35 μmol cm−2 day−1 for calcifying and fleshy, respectively, mean ± SE; Wilcoxon p=0.0001 for comparisons between fleshy vs controls and vs coral).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: Fleshy macroalgae had the highest fraction of net photosynthetic O2 released in the form of gas (37.33 ± 8.34%), followed by turf algae (13.78 ± 1.33%), CCA (10.19 ± 2.88%), and corals (5.00 ± 5.55%).
source: Fleshy macroalgae had the highest fraction of net photosynthetic O2 (sum of dissolved and gaseous O2) released in the form of gas (37.33 ± 8.34%), followed by turf algae (13.78 ± 1.33%), CCA (10.19 ± 2.88%), and corals (5.00 ± 5.55%) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The difference in the fraction of O2 accumulated as gas was significant among treatments and higher in fleshy organisms.
source: The difference in the fraction of O2 accumulated as gas was significant among treatments (Kruskal-Wallis χ2(4)=29.2, p=7.067e-06), being higher in fleshy organisms (Kruskal-Wallis χ2(2)=26.3, p=1.904e-06; Wilcoxon p<9.5e-05 for fleshy vs calcifying).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: The green fleshy algae Chaetomorpha had the highest bubble production rates (10.3 ± 0.45 bubbles per min per dm2).
source: The green fleshy algae Chaetomorpha had the highest bubble production rates (10.3 ± 0.45 bubbles per min per dm2, mean ± SE; Video 1), followed by the fleshy red algae Gracilaria sp. (1.29 ± 1.21 bubbles per min per dm2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from open-tank experiments

claim: Bubble production by the two coral species analyzed was close to zero.
source: Bubble production by the two coral species analyzed was close to zero (0.1 ± 0.14 and 0.006 ± 0.02 bubbles per min per dm2 for Favia sp. and Montipora sp., respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from open-tank experiments

claim: Ebullition rate was significantly higher in fleshy compared to calcifying organisms.
source: Ebullition rate was significantly higher in fleshy compared to calcifying organisms (Kruskal-Wallis χ2(3)=349.46, p =<2.2e-16; Wilcoxon p<2e-16 for fleshy vs calcifying).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical tests

claim: Bubbles were observed forming on the algal surfaces, detaching and rising to the atmosphere starting as early as 20 min into the experiment.
source: Bubbles were observed forming on the algal surfaces, detaching and rising to the atmosphere starting as early as 20 min into the experiment.
evidence: Supported by direct observation during experiments

claim: The dissolved oxygen concentration increased through the course of the incubations.
source: The dissolved oxygen concentration also increased through the course of the incubations (Figure 5B), however, there was no relationship between the rate of bubble production and the dissolved oxygen concentration (linear regression p=0.16, R2 = 0.04) or the change in oxygen concentration over time (linear regression p=0.27, R2 = 0.03).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical tests

claim: There was no relationship between the rate of bubble production and the dissolved oxygen concentration.
source: The dissolved oxygen concentration also increased through the course of the incubations (Figure 5B), however, there was no relationship between the rate of bubble production and the dissolved oxygen concentration (linear regression p=0.16, R2 = 0.04) or the change in oxygen concentration over time (linear regression p=0.27, R2 = 0.03).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis with p-value and R-squared

claim: There was no relationship between the rate of bubble production and the change in oxygen concentration over time.
source: The dissolved oxygen concentration also increased through the course of the incubations (Figure 5B), however, there was no relationship between the rate of bubble production and the dissolved oxygen concentration (linear regression p=0.16, R2 = 0.04) or the change in oxygen concentration over time (linear regression p=0.27, R2 = 0.03).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis with p-value and R-squared

claim: The mean bubble diameter produced by the algae Gracilaria sp. was larger than that produced by the algae Chaetomorpha sp.
source: The mean bubble diameter produced by the algae Gracialaria sp. was larger than that produced by the algae Chaetomorpha sp. (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; 0.79 ± 27 mm in diameter and 0.64 ± 0.23 mm for Gracialaria sp. and Chaetomorpha sp., respectively, however these differences were not statistically significant).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: At 300 µmol quanta m−2 s−1, the algae Chaetomorpha sp. had the highest ebullition rates (16.2 ± 1.9 bubbles per min per dm2).
source: The incubation of these same algae species at higher PAR values (300 to 650 µmol quanta m−2 s−1, normally observed on a reef in a sunny day) yielded different bubble production rates: at 300 µmol quanta m−2 s−1, the algae Chaetomorpha sp. had the highest ebullition rates (Figure 5C and Video 2, 16.2 ± 1.9 bubbles per min per dm2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Video 2

claim: The ebullition rate of Chaetomorpha sp. decreased to 0.9 ± 0.04 at 650 µmol quanta m−2 s−1.
source: The rate decreased to 0.9 ± 0.04 at 650 µmol quanta m−2 s−1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The algae Gracilaria sp. also produced fewer bubbles per minute at 650 µmol quanta m−2 s−1 (0.9 ± 0.08).
source: The algae Gracilaria sp. also produced fewer bubbles per minute at 650 µmol quanta m−2 s−1 (0.9 ± 0.08).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: At 0% algal cover, 10.4% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes.
source: At 0% algal cover, 10.4% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes, compared to 35.9% at 50% algal cover, and 47.0% at 100% algal cover.
evidence: Predicted by the weighted linear model incorporating experimental data

claim: At 50% algal cover, 35.9% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes.
source: At 0% algal cover, 10.4% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes, compared to 35.9% at 50% algal cover, and 47.0% at 100% algal cover.
evidence: Predicted by the weighted linear model incorporating experimental data

claim: At 100% algal cover, 47.0% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes.
source: At 0% algal cover, 10.4% of the benthic oxygen production is consumed by microbes, compared to 35.9% at 50% algal cover, and 47.0% at 100% algal cover.
evidence: Predicted by the weighted linear model incorporating experimental data

claim: The amount of oxygen loss by ebullition is predicted to increase from 1.0% at 0% algal cover to 14.0% at 50% algal cover and 19.7% at 100% algae cover.
source: The amount of oxygen loss by ebullition is predicted to increase from 1.0% at 0% algal cover to 14.0% at 50% algal cover and 19.7% at 100% algae cover.
evidence: Predicted by the weighted linear model incorporating experimental data

claim: Combined, microbial respiration and ebullition are predicted to consume 50% of the gross oxygen production at 50% algal cover, and 66.7% of the oxygen production at 100% algal cover.
source: Combined, microbial respiration and ebullition are predicted to consume 50% of the gross oxygen production at 50% algal cover, and 66.7% of the oxygen production at 100% algal cover.
evidence: Predicted by the weighted linear model incorporating experimental data

claim: A physiological transition to overflow metabolisms is the underlying mechanism of bacterial biomass accumulation observed in coral reefs.
source: The work presented here shows that a physiological transition to overflow metabolisms is the underlying mechanism of bacterial biomass accumulation observed in coral reefs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined metagenomic and experimental results

claim: The loss of oxygen through ebullition facilitates overflow metabolism and adds to the effect of high microbial respiration that depletes oxygen in algae-dominated systems.
source: The loss of oxygen through ebullition facilitates this type of metabolism and adds to the effect of high microbial respiration that depletes oxygen in otherwise oxygen-rich, algae-dominated systems.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results on ebullition and microbial metabolism

claim: The abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in the Pentose Phosphate (PP) and Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathways increased with fleshy algae cover.
source: The abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in the Pentose Phosphate (PP) and Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathways, increased with fleshy algae cover (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by metagenomic data shown in Figure 1

claim: NADH preferentially donates electrons to oxidative phosphorylation that consumes oxygen during ATP production.
source: These two reduced coenzymes have distinct cell fates, with NADH preferentially donating electrons to oxidative phosphorylation that consumes oxygen during ATP production (Pollak et al., 2007; Spaans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pollak et al., 2007; Spaans et al., 2015

claim: Cells utilizing more NADPH pathways consume less O2 relative to carbon compared to cells utilizing more NADH, and store a larger fraction of the consumed carbon into biomass.
source: Thus, cells utilizing more NADPH pathways consume less O2 relative to carbon compared to cells utilizing more NADH, and store a larger fraction of the consumed carbon into biomass.
evidence: Inferred from established biochemical knowledge about NADPH and NADH pathways

claim: The TCA cycle can work as a biosynthetic pathway by providing intermediates to amino acids, nitrogenous bases and fatty acids syntheses.
source: But the TCA cycle can work as a biosynthetic pathway by providing intermediates to amino acids, nitrogenous bases and fatty acids syntheses (Cronan and Laporte, 2013; Sauer and Eikmanns, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cronan and Laporte, 2013; Sauer and Eikmanns, 2005

claim: TCA cycle stoichiometry is maintained through the resupply of intermediates by anaplerotic reactions that use pyruvate (or phosphoenolpyruvate).
source: TCA cycle stoichiometry is maintained through the resupply of these intermediates by anaplerotic reactions that use pyruvate (or phosphoenolpyruvate) (Owen et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Owen et al., 2002

claim: The abundance of genes encoding anaplerotic enzymes increased, and genes encoding an oxidative decarboxylation step in the Krebs cycle decreased with increasing algal cover.
source: In the reefs analyzed here, the abundance of genes encoding anaplerotic enzymes increased, and genes encoding an oxidative decarboxylation step in the Krebs cycle decreased with increasing algal cover.
evidence: Supported by metagenomic data analysis
